section.title: The Ten Lepers and the Coming Kingdom
section.sectionRationale: Jesus warns against causing little ones to stumble and calls for endless forgiveness, then answers the plea for more faith by pointing to faith as small as a seed and to servants who claim no merit. On the road He heals ten lepers, but only one, a Samaritan, returns to give thanks. Asked when the kingdom will come, He says it is already in their midst, and He describes the sudden, unmistakable day of the Son of Man, which will come like lightning after He has first suffered and been rejected.
section.thesis: The kingdom is already present in the person of Jesus and will one day break in suddenly and universally, so its people are to forgive without limit, trust with humble faith, return in grateful worship, and lose their lives to keep them, ready for the day of the Son of Man.
section.frameNote: Four movements: stumbling blocks and unlimited forgiveness; faith like a seed and unworthy servants; the ten lepers and the grateful Samaritan; and the coming of the kingdom and the day of the Son of Man.

verses.text: Jesus said to His disciples, “It is inevitable that {{skandalon|stumbling blocks}} will come, but woe to the one through whom they come!
It would be better for him to have a millstone hung around his neck and to be thrown into the sea than to cause one of these little ones to stumble.
Watch yourselves. If your brother sins, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him.
Even if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times returns to say, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive him.”

units.label: Faith like a seed and unworthy servants
units.note: we have only done our duty

verses.text: The apostles said to the Lord, “Increase our {{pistis|faith}}!”
And the Lord answered, “If you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you can say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it will obey you.
Which of you whose servant comes in from plowing or shepherding in the field will say to him, ‘Come at once and sit down to eat’?
Instead, won’t he tell him, ‘Prepare my meal and dress yourself to serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you may eat and drink’?
Does he thank the servant because he did what he was told?
So you also, when you have done everything commanded of you, should say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done our duty.’”

units.label: The ten lepers and the grateful Samaritan
units.note: was no one found to return except this foreigner

verses.text: While Jesus was on His way to Jerusalem, He was passing between Samaria and Galilee.
As He entered one of the villages, He was met by ten lepers. They stood at a distance
and raised their voices, shouting, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!”
When Jesus saw them, He said, “Go, show yourselves to the priests.” And as they were on their way, they were cleansed.
When one of them saw that he was healed, he came back, praising God in a loud voice.
He fell facedown at Jesus’ feet in thanksgiving to Him, and he was a Samaritan.
“Were not all ten cleansed?” Jesus asked. “Where then are the other nine?
Was no one found except this foreigner to return and give glory to God?”
Then Jesus said to him, “Rise and go; your faith has made you {{sozo|well}}!”

units.label: The coming of the kingdom and the day of the Son of Man
units.note: as the lightning flashes, so will the Son of Man be

verses.text: When asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, Jesus replied, “The kingdom of God will not come with observable signs.
Nor will people say, ‘Look, here it is,’ or ‘There it is.’ For you see, the kingdom of God is {{entos|in your midst}}.”
Then He said to the disciples, “The time is coming when you will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man, but you will not see it.
People will tell you, ‘Look, there He is!’ or ‘Look, here He is!’ Do not go out or chase after them.
For just as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one end to the other, so will be the Son of Man in His day.
But first He must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.
Just as it was in the days of Noah, so also will it be in the days of the Son of Man:
People were eating and drinking, marrying and being given in marriage, up to the day Noah entered the ark. Then the flood came and destroyed them all.
It was the same in the days of Lot: People were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building.
But on the day Lot left Sodom, fire and sulfur rained down from heaven and destroyed them all.
It will be just like that on the day the Son of Man is revealed.
On that day, let no one on the housetop come down to retrieve his possessions. Likewise, let no one in the field return for anything he has left behind.
Remember Lot’s wife!
Whoever tries to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will preserve it.
I tell you, on that night two people will be in one bed: one will be taken and the other left.
Two women will be grinding grain together: one will be taken and the other left.”
“Where, Lord?” they asked. Jesus answered, “Wherever there is a carcass, there the vultures will gather.”

skandalon.gloss: A stumbling block, a snare, that which trips another into sin. Jesus warns that such things will inevitably come in a fallen world, but woe to the one who causes a little one to stumble. Disciples must watch themselves, for leading the weak into sin is a grave and fearful thing.

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust. The apostles ask for more of it as if it were a quantity, but Jesus answers that faith the size of a mustard seed can uproot a tree. What matters is not the amount but the object: even the smallest true trust, resting on God, is mighty because of the One it holds.

sozo.gloss: To save, to heal, to make whole. Ten were cleansed of leprosy, but only the returning Samaritan hears, your faith has saved you, the word reaching beyond the body to the whole person. Gratitude and faith carry him past healing into salvation, a wholeness the other nine did not receive.

entos.gloss: Within, in the midst of, among. The kingdom of God, Jesus says, is entos of them, already present in His own person and work rather than arriving with a spectacle to be spotted. The King stands among them, so the kingdom is nearer than they think, not out on some future horizon alone.

basic.context: Jesus warns His disciples that things which trip people into sin will come, but woe to the one who causes a little one to stumble; better a millstone and the sea. He commands endless forgiveness of the repentant brother, even seven times a day. When the apostles beg for more faith, He says faith as small as a mustard seed can uproot a tree, and that servants who obey should claim no merit but say, we have only done our duty. On the road ten lepers cry for mercy and are cleansed as they go, but only one, a Samaritan foreigner, returns to fall at Jesus' feet in thanks, and to him alone Jesus says, your faith has made you well. Asked when the kingdom will come, He answers that it is already in their midst, and He warns that the day of the Son of Man will come suddenly like lightning, after He first suffers and is rejected.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter gathers short teachings on life in the kingdom, forgiveness, humble faith, gratitude, then turns to the kingdom's presence and future. The healing of the ten dramatizes the difference between being cleansed and coming back in worship. The eschatology warns against both false alarms and complacency: the day is certain, sudden, and preceded by the cross.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus warns of the skandalon, the stumbling block that trips the weak into sin. Faith, pistis, need not be great in quantity, only real, for a seed's worth can move a tree. To the grateful Samaritan He says your faith has sozo you, saved and made you whole, more than the healing the nine received. And the kingdom of God is entos, in their midst, present in the King Himself.
basic.typology: The cleansed leper sent to the priest recalls Leviticus and points to Christ our true cleansing. The days of Noah and Lot become patterns of a world caught unaware by sudden judgment. Lot's wife, looking back, warns against clinging to the doomed old life when God calls us out.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Master whom the lepers call on for mercy and the One at whose feet the Samaritan worships, receiving thanks that belongs to God. He is the Son of Man who must first suffer and be rejected, then be revealed like lightning across the sky. And He is the King in whose presence the kingdom of God has already come into their midst.
basic.god: God is worthy of endless forgiveness passed on to others and of grateful worship returned to Him. He is the God whose kingdom comes not as spectacle but in His Son, and who will one day judge the world suddenly, as in the days of Noah and Lot. He asks humble service that claims no merit and glad thanksgiving that gives Him glory.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 18 gives the parallel on forgiving the brother. Leviticus 14 sets the law of cleansing the leper. Genesis 19 tells of Lot, Sodom, and his wife. 1 Thessalonians 5 says the day of the Lord comes like a thief, sudden and unexpected.
basic.oneStory: As Jesus nears Jerusalem, He teaches His people to forgive, to trust, and to return in gratitude, and He reveals that the kingdom has already arrived in Him while its consummation waits for the day of the Son of Man. That day will come suddenly, after the cross, so the story presses us to lose our lives now in order to keep them then.

context.literary:
Luke 17 reads like a collection of sayings and then a story and then a discourse, yet the pieces are placed with care. The opening unit, 17:1-10, is addressed to the disciples and moves in a chain: do not cause a little one to stumble, rebuke and forgive a brother, and then, when the apostles ask for more faith, learn what faith can do and what a servant owes. The second unit, 17:11-19, is a narrative, the only one in the chapter, and it shows the abstractions at work: a company of outcasts asks for mercy, one comes back, and he is the one least expected. The third, 17:20-37, turns from the present kingdom to the future day.

The narrative is set within Luke's long journey. Luke has marked the road to Jerusalem at 9:51, at 13:22, and again here at 17:11, with the note that Jesus was 'passing between Samaria and Galilee.' The geography is odd for a straight road and sets the story on a border, where Jew and Samaritan meet. The border is the right place for a story about a Samaritan who proves more faithful than those who share Jesus' birth.

The healing has a quiet progression in its verbs. In 17:14 the ten are 'cleansed' on the way, in 17:15 the one 'saw that he was healed,' and in 17:19 Jesus says that his faith has made him 'well.' The nine received the first, the one received all three. The structure of the story also depends on Jesus' questions in 17:17-18, 'Were not all ten cleansed? Where then are the other nine?' which are questions the narrator leaves for the reader.

The last section runs on a pattern of contrasts. The kingdom comes without observable signs, 17:20, yet the day of the Son of Man will be as plain as lightning, 17:24. Between those two statements sits the saying that He must first suffer, 17:25, the hinge on which the chapter turns. The comparisons to Noah and Lot, 17:26-30, take up a similar double structure of ordinary life interrupted by sudden judgment. The discourse closes with the puzzling saying of the carcass and the birds, which the disciples ask about and which Jesus answers with an image and no explanation.
context.historical:
The ten stand at a distance, 17:12, because the law required it. Leviticus 13:45-46 told the person with a defiling skin disease to live alone outside the camp and to cry out a warning. The BSB footnote at 17:12 notes that 'leper' meant a person with a skin disease and points to Leviticus 13. The disease in view covered a range of conditions, not only what we now call leprosy. A cleansing was formally declared by a priest, and Leviticus 14:1-32 sets out the procedure, which is why Jesus tells them to go and show themselves to the priests, 17:14. The order is a test of trust: they are sent before they are healed, and they are cleansed as they go.

In their shared affliction the ten were a mixed company. Jews and Samaritans, who had little to do with each other, were thrown together by the same exclusion. The hostility between the two peoples was old. It went back to the settlement of foreign peoples in Samaria after the fall of the northern kingdom, 2 Kings 17:24-41, and to the rival worship on Mount Gerizim. John 4:9 says plainly that Jews do not associate with Samaritans, and Luke has told of a Samaritan village refusing Jesus, 9:51-56, and of the Samaritan who helped the man left half dead, 10:25-37. Jesus' words to the grateful man, 'this foreigner,' 17:18, imply that the other nine were Israelites.

The question the Pharisees ask in 17:20 reflects a people living in expectation. Many longed for the arrival of God's kingdom, and some sought signs or a date. Luke 19:11 says explicitly that the crowd supposed the kingdom was about to appear at once. Jesus' answer redirects that expectation.

The days of Noah and of Lot were firmly fixed in Jewish memory as pictures of judgment that overtook a world at ease, Genesis 6:5-8:22 and 19:1-29. The 'housetop' of 17:31 evokes the flat roofs of houses, where a person might be at midday, and the 'two women grinding grain' of 17:35 is a household scene: grinding was done by hand at a mill by women. The BSB omits verse 36, noting in a footnote that a later text includes it, and it matches the parallel at Matthew 24:40.
context.canonical:
The healing of the ten echoes two earlier stories of leprosy. In 2 Kings 5, Naaman the Syrian, a foreigner, is told by Elisha to wash in the Jordan, and he is cleansed after he obeys a word he had hoped would be more dramatic. Then he returns to the man of God to give thanks, 2 Kings 5:15. Jesus had already pointed to Naaman in the synagogue at Nazareth, saying that there were many with leprosy in Israel in Elisha's time and none was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian, Luke 4:27. The Samaritan of 17:16 is the second Naaman, and the way that the foreigner returns to the one who healed him repeats the older story.

The law of the leper in Leviticus 13 and 14 stands behind the instruction to show oneself to the priests, and Jesus' ministry has already included cleansing a leper and sending him to the priest, Luke 5:12-14, and the report to John that lepers are cleansed, 7:22. Isaiah 35 had pictured the healing of the blind and lame as a sign of the age to come.

The kingdom's presence is spoken of in Luke 10:9, 'The kingdom of God has come near,' and in 11:20, where Jesus says that if He drives out demons by the finger of God then the kingdom has come upon them. The coming day of the Son of Man draws on Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds and receives a kingdom. Luke 21:25-28 and 22:69 return to the title. Paul says that the kingdom of God is righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit, Romans 14:17.

Noah and Lot appear again in 2 Peter 2:5-9, where God's rescue of the righteous is joined with the punishment of the wicked, and in Matthew 24:37-41, where the days of Noah are the pattern for the coming of the Son of Man. Paul compares the day of the Lord to a thief, 1 Thessalonians 5:2-3. The teaching on forgiveness repeats Matthew 18:15-22, and on faith Matthew 17:20 and Mark 11:22-24.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants a people who can live between the present and the future. The first half of the chapter describes a community that hurts and forgives: stumbling blocks will come, so the disciple must be watchful that he is never one; offenses will happen, so the disciple must be ready to forgive more times than seems reasonable. It is a picture of life under a king who has already forgiven. The apostles' request for more faith shows how heavy that standard feels, and Jesus' answer is not a technique but a reorientation. What they need is not an increase but the thing itself, and it works through obedience, not accounting.

The story of the ten lepers invites Luke's readers, many of whom were outsiders to Israel, to see themselves in the Samaritan. They are to notice that the greatest healing was not the clearing of skin but the return of a man to the feet of Jesus, giving glory to God. The healing alone was shared by ten; what Jesus calls faith and wellness belonged to one.

The final section is written to correct two mistakes at once. Some were looking for a visible kingdom to arrive on a date, and Jesus says it is already among them in His person. Others, after the cross, would long to see the Son of Man and would be tempted by every report of Him. Luke tells them to wait and not to chase rumors, because the day will be as plain as lightning, and to live now with the loosened grip of people who remember Lot's wife.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The sayings on stumbling, forgiveness, faith and duty are imperatives: watch yourselves, rebuke, forgive, say that you are unworthy servants. They are not descriptions of what usually happens. The seven times in a day, 17:4, is a figure for a forgiveness that does not keep a count. It is not a command to ignore repentance, since the text says the brother returns and says 'I repent,' and a rebuke comes first, 17:3.

The parable of the servants in 17:7-10 describes a master and a slave and is not an endorsement of slavery. It is a short illustration that borrows the ordinary relation to make a point about merit. The prescription is not that God is a harsh employer but that no obedience is a claim on Him. It is also easily misused: the line should not be read as a license to withhold thanks from those who serve, since the next scene condemns the failure of gratitude.

The healing of the ten narrates an event but its teaching is by example. Nowhere is the story turned into a command, yet the contrast between the one and the nine is plain. The gratitude of the Samaritan is the thing Jesus names and commends. It is therefore fair to apply the story: to return, to give glory to God, and to fall at Jesus' feet.

The sayings about the day of the Son of Man describe what will happen and prescribe how to wait. The pictures of Noah and Lot are not given to calculate a date but to warn of unreadiness, and the command about the housetop and Lot's wife is not a rule for fleeing but an image of letting go of possessions. The instruction not to chase after reports of His coming is a command still needed. It keeps the church from both panic and speculation.

debates.question: What does Jesus mean that the kingdom of God is 'in your midst'?

views.label: Present in the person and work of Jesus among them
views.case: Spoken to hostile Pharisees, 'within you' is unlikely to mean inside their hearts; the natural sense is that the kingdom stands among them in the King Himself, already breaking in through His words and works rather than arriving as a spectacle to be spotted.

views.label: A reality to be received inwardly
views.case: The phrase can be rendered 'within you' or 'within your grasp', stressing that the kingdom is not a matter of external observation but of inward reception and response. On this reading Jesus points them away from sign-watching to the rule of God that must be welcomed personally.

debates.bearing: Either way Jesus redirects them from looking for a future spectacle to reckoning with the King already present, whose reign is to be recognized and received now.

debates.question: What is the 'taken' and 'left' of the day of the Son of Man?

views.label: Taken in judgment, left in safety
views.case: The context is Noah and Lot, where the flood and the fire took the unready away in judgment while the righteous were preserved; 'destroyed them all' frames the taking as removal in judgment, so to be left is to be spared.

views.label: Taken to be with the Lord, left behind for judgment
views.case: Read alongside the gathering of the elect elsewhere, some understand the taking as being gathered to Christ and the leaving as exclusion from His salvation. On this view being taken is the blessing.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree on the urgent point: the day divides humanity suddenly and finally, so the call is to be ready now, holding this life loosely, remembering Lot's wife.

debates.question: What do the carcass and the vultures in verse 37 mean?

views.label: Judgment will be as unmistakable as the gathering of birds to a corpse
views.case: The disciples ask where, and Jesus answers with a proverb-like image: wherever there is a body, the birds gather. The point is that no one will need to be told where to look, since the day will be as plain as the lightning of 17:24, and that judgment falls where death already is.

views.label: The elect will be gathered to the Son of Man
views.case: Others hear the image as one of gathering, with the question 'where' answered by 'wherever He is.' The Greek word that the BSB renders 'vultures' is often translated 'eagles,' which some link to the gathering of the elect, while the carcass or body is taken by some to mean Christ Himself.

debates.bearing: The saying is obscure and the readings differ, but they agree that the day will need no guide. For the reader the application is not to speculate on locations but to be ready, as Jesus says in the verses before.

study.originalLanguages:
Luke 17:1 says that stumbling blocks will come, and the Greek behind 'it is inevitable' is a striking phrase that means, literally, that it is impossible for them not to come. The text does not excuse those through whom they come; the woe that follows is the heavier for the inevitability. The little ones of 17:2 are mikroi, the small, and the stone hung around the neck is a millstone, a heavy stone, which makes the image one of sinking.

The instruction in 17:3 to 'rebuke' is the verb epitimao. Luke uses it of Jesus' rebuke of a fever, a storm and demons, 4:39, 8:24 and 4:35, and here for a brother's rebuke of a brother. The word is not a gentle one, but it is in the service of the brother, and the forgiveness that follows uses aphiemi, 'to let go, release, forgive,' the same verb as in the Lord's Prayer, 11:4. In 17:4 the offender 'returns' to say 'I repent.' The verb is epistrepho, to turn back, and the verb for repenting is metanoeo. A person who turns and repents is one who has done what the Samaritan will do in 17:15 when he 'came back,' and the same Greek verb for turning is used. The apology and the thanksgiving belong to one family of movements.

When the apostles ask the Lord to 'increase' their faith, 17:5, the literal request is to 'add' faith, as one adds to a pile. Jesus' reply in 17:6 begins with 'if,' and in the Greek the form of the condition, an 'if' with the indicative followed by a verb with the particle an, is commonly read as a condition contrary to fact, 'if you had faith as a mustard seed, you would be saying.' On that reading, which is widely held, Jesus gently says that they do not have even that. The mulberry in the saying is a sykaminos, a tree distinct from the sycamore fig of 19:4, and the command to be uprooted and planted in the sea is an image of the impossible.

The servant in 17:10 is called achreios, a word that is hard to render. 'Unworthy' is the BSB's choice. It can mean useless, unprofitable, or one who has no claim, and the same word appears in Matthew 25:30. The following clause says 'we have done what we ought,' using the verb opheilo, 'to owe,' the verb of debt in 11:4. The servant has paid what was owed and has earned nothing beyond it. In 17:8 the servant is told to 'dress himself,' the verb of girding up for service, and Luke 12:37 uses the same verb of the Master who dresses Himself to serve His watching servants.

The cry of the lepers in 17:13 addresses Jesus as epistata, 'Master,' a word used in the New Testament only by Luke and, except here, only by disciples. The lepers use the disciples' title. In 17:15 and 17:18 the Samaritan glorifies God, from doxazo, and Luke has used the same word of the paralytic in 5:25, the woman in 13:13 and the blind man in 18:43. The one who is healed gives glory to God. In 17:16 he gives thanks with the verb eucharisteo, the verb that Luke uses for Jesus' giving of thanks at the Supper, 22:19, and for the Pharisee's thanks in 18:11, so that the same verb carries the pattern of true and false gratitude.

In 17:20 the kingdom does not come 'with observable signs.' The noun is parateresis, built on the verb that Luke used for those who 'watched Him closely' in 6:7, 14:1 and 20:20. The Pharisees have been watching Jesus, and He tells them that the kingdom is not something that can be watched. In 17:24 'lightning' is astrape, the word of 10:18. In 17:25 the Son of Man 'must' suffer, the verb dei of divine necessity, which Luke uses for the Passion in 9:22 and 24:26, and He is 'rejected,' apodokimazo, the same verb as in 9:22. In 17:30 the Son of Man is 'revealed,' apokalypto, from which 'apocalypse' comes. And in 17:33 the saving of life uses peripoieomai, to secure for oneself, a verb that Acts 20:28 uses of God acquiring the church with His own blood. Whoever tries to secure his life will lose it, and the God who secured His people with His own blood is the one who gives life.

typology.type: Naaman the Syrian, cleansed and returning, 2 Kings 5:1-15
typology.fulfillment: Naaman was a foreign leper cleansed by obeying a prophet's word, and he came back to give thanks and confess that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel. Jesus already pointed to him in Luke 4:27, and the Samaritan of 17:11-19 repeats the pattern. The correspondence escalates because the one who speaks is not a prophet but the Lord, at whose feet the Samaritan falls, and the thanks he gives are given to Jesus, 17:16, as well as to God, 17:15. The type falls short in that Naaman returned to a man of God who refused a gift, while the Samaritan falls before one who is the giver of the healing.

typology.type: The leper sent to the priest, Leviticus 14:1-32
typology.fulfillment: The law provided that someone cleansed of a skin disease should be examined by a priest and offer sacrifices. Jesus sends the ten as they are, with the cleansing still to come, as He did in Luke 5:14. The correspondence deepens in Hebrews, where Christ is the great high priest who is also the sacrifice, Hebrews 4:14 and 9:11-14, and where His blood cleanses the conscience from dead works. The type falls short in the need for repeated offerings and the separation of the unclean from the camp, while Christ cleanses once for all and Himself goes outside the camp to bear reproach, Hebrews 13:12-13.

Noah's world went about its business and the flood took them all, while Noah and his household were carried through in an ark. Jesus makes it the pattern for the day of the Son of Man, Luke 17:26-27, and Peter does the same, 2 Peter 3:5-7. The correspondence in Christ is rescue through judgment: Peter says that those in the ark were brought safely through water and that baptism now saves through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, 1 Peter 3:20-21. The type falls short because the flood was a judgment by water and a promise never to repeat it, Genesis 9:11, while the final day is a judgment by fire and the end of the old order, 2 Peter 3:10.

Lot's wife looked back at Sodom and became a pillar of salt. Jesus gives her three words, 'Remember Lot's wife,' in 17:32, as a warning against clinging to what God is leaving behind. The correspondence runs to every disciple who is called to leave something, and it fits with the sayings on losing and saving life in 17:33. In Christ the call is not only to leave but to follow, as Hebrews 11:15-16 says, desiring a better country. The type is partial in that Lot's wife is a picture of loss alone, while Christ promises that whoever loses his life will preserve it.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ by showing who He is among the people who come to Him. The ten lepers call Him 'Master,' and He sends them as a Lord who commands cleansing by a word. The Samaritan falls at His feet and gives thanks to Him, and Jesus accepts it, which for a faithful Jew would be an astonishing thing to receive unless the one receiving it were the presence of God. Luke has just told us that the man glorified God in a loud voice and then fell at the feet of Jesus; the two actions are placed together, and Jesus asks why only a foreigner returned to give glory to God.

He is the one who serves. In the parable of the servant, 17:7-10, the servant dresses himself to serve his master. In Luke 12:37 the same language is used of the Master Himself: He will dress Himself, make His servants recline, and come and serve them. And at the Last Supper He says that He is among them as the one who serves, 22:27. The disciple who says 'we are unworthy servants' is describing the correct place before a master who then reverses the roles. John 13:4-5 shows the reversal with a towel around the waist.

He is the Son of Man who must suffer. 'But first He must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation,' 17:25, is a statement at the heart of Luke's theology. The word 'must' is the necessity of God's plan, which Luke repeats in 9:22 and 24:26. The glory of the Son of Man in Daniel 7:13-14 passes through a cross, and the chapter will not allow the day of lightning to be separated from the Passion. No one who wishes to see His day can skip what comes first.

He is also the presence of the kingdom. When He says that it is in their midst, 17:21, He is not only describing but pointing at Himself. The King is standing in the crowd of Pharisees, and the sign is not lightning but a Man who heals ten lepers. The kingdom of God is present where the Samaritan kneels, where a brother is forgiven seven times, and where a seed of faith obeys.

And He is the one who gives the saving that the nine did not receive. The nine were cleansed; the one was made 'well,' and the Greek verb is the one that also means saved, as the BSB footnote notes. To be cleansed is to be given a gift, but to return and fall at Jesus' feet is to receive Him. The reading should avoid forcing details: the ten are not a code, and the nine are not a picture of a specific group. What the story shows is that the way to Christ is open to those who come back to Him, and that He is the One at whose feet they come.
study.god:
The God of Luke 17 is a God of mercy and of command. The ten lepers appeal for mercy and receive an order, 'Go, show yourselves to the priests,' and the healing arrives as they obey. God's mercy is not a feeling but an act, and it asks for trust that moves before it sees the result. In the same chapter, the instruction to forgive a brother seven times in a day is an instruction to imitate God, who forgives repeatedly. The standard is high because the one who sets it has already been generous.

He is a God who is owed everything and who refuses to be a debtor. The parable of the servants, 17:7-10, insists that no service puts God in our debt. This does not make Him cold. It guards the grace of the gospel: the service of believers is a response and never a payment. The God who is owed nothing by creatures is the God who gives, as the Samaritan's cleansing shows, and who values a thank-you as the right response to a gift.

He is a God who is glorified by gratitude. The Samaritan comes back praising God in a loud voice, and Jesus asks why no one else returned to give glory to God. The question reveals what God seeks from people He has healed: to be recognized as the giver. The nine were obedient and cleansed, and they were not condemned, but they missed the center of the gift. Worship that is thankful, voiced aloud and falling face down is the thing Jesus names.

He is a God who comes in His Son without display. The kingdom does not come with observable signs, and the God of Israel stands among the Pharisees in the form of a Galilean teacher. The same God will one day come as the lightning that lights up the sky from one end to the other. This is a God who is both hidden and revealed, who works quietly now and who will be seen by all.

He is a God of judgment. The days of Noah and Lot are not mentioned lightly. People were eating and drinking and building, and judgment came without negotiation. The God of the Gospels is the God of the flood and of the fire on Sodom, and these are the same God who sends rain on the just and the unjust. He rescues Noah and Lot. His judgment is certain and sudden, and His rescue is certain also.

For worship the chapter asks us to forgive without a count, to trust without a measurement, to give thanks aloud, and to hold this life loosely, because the God we serve is both present in His Son and coming in glory.

crossReferences.note: Naaman, a foreign commander, is healed of leprosy when he obeys Elisha's word and returns to give thanks. Jesus had already cited him in Luke 4:27, and the Samaritan leper of Luke 17 repeats his story: a foreigner cleansed and grateful where Israelites were not.

The law lays out how a person cleansed of a skin disease is examined by the priest and offers sacrifices. Jesus' command to the ten in Luke 17:14 sends them into this procedure, and the BSB footnote at 17:14 points to it.

In the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus says that there were many lepers in Israel in Elisha's time and none was cleansed but Naaman the Syrian. The listeners were enraged, and the story of Luke 17 plays out the same point, showing that a foreigner often responds where the privileged do not.

A Samaritan is the one who shows mercy to the man left half dead. Together with Luke 17:16, the story shows Luke's steady pattern of making a Samaritan the example for those who consider themselves insiders.

The Master dresses Himself to serve the servants who are ready when He comes. It reverses the picture in Luke 17:7-10 of a servant dressing to serve a master, and the contrast shows that the Lord of the parable is also the one who serves.

If Jesus drives out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon the hearers. It explains how the kingdom can be 'in your midst' in Luke 17:21: it is present where the King is working.

One like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and is given dominion, glory and a kingdom. This is the background of the day of the Son of Man in Luke 17:22-30, and the 'must first suffer' of verse 25 shows how Jesus joins that vision to the Passion.

Lot is urged to flee Sodom and not to look back, and his wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. This is the story behind the three words of Luke 17:32, a warning against clinging to what God is judging.

The days of Noah are made the pattern for the coming of the Son of Man, with two in the field, one taken and one left. It is a close parallel to Luke 17:26-35, and reading them together helps with the taken and the left.

Peter asks how many times he should forgive, and Jesus says seventy-seven times. The two texts make the same point from different directions: the disciple's forgiveness is not to be counted, and Luke 17:4 sets the same standard in the form of seven times in a day.

The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night, when people say there is peace and security. Paul uses the same picture of a sudden day on a complacent world that Luke 17:26-30 uses in the days of Noah and Lot.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a world in which there is no uncleanness, no exile and no stumbling block. Genesis 3 changes that. The man and the woman are driven from the garden, and the story from then on is of people separated from the presence of God. The leper at a distance, crying out, is a picture of that separation, a person who must live outside the camp. In Luke 17 the ten stand where all of humanity stood, at a distance, and they raise their voices to the one who can help.

Israel's law gave the separated a path back through the priest. The prophets kept alive the hope of a day when the lame would walk and the blind would see. The story of Naaman, in which a foreign leper is cleansed and returns in thanks, shows that God's mercy was never limited to Israel. When Jesus meets the ten on the border between Samaria and Galilee, the old promises are being kept in a way that crosses borders.

The kingdom that the prophets looked for is in the middle of the story. Jesus says that it is in the midst of those who ask about it. The one who forgives, who heals, and who sends cleansed people on their way is the one in whom God's rule is arriving. The Samaritan sees it, and he is made well. This is the first side of the kingdom: already present.

The second side is not yet. The Son of Man must suffer and be rejected before He is revealed, and so the days of the church are days of waiting. Luke has the disciples long to see one of the days of the Son of Man and be unable to. The chapter gives them what to do in that interval: forgive, believe, give thanks, and let go of the life that clings. Acts then shows the church doing these things, with the day of His appearing in view, Acts 1:11.

The story ends with the day that the chapter describes. The Son of Man will be as plain as the lightning, and the world that carried on eating and drinking will be judged, while the faithful are gathered. In the new creation, nothing is unclean, and no one stands at a distance. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4. God dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3. The people who once stood far off will come near, and they will give glory to God with a loud voice, as the Samaritan did, face down at the feet of the one who made them well.

quiz.q: How does Jesus tell His disciples to treat a brother who sins and repents?

options.text: To forgive him, even seven times in a day, whenever he repents.
options.note: Luke 17:3-4 commands repeated, tireless forgiveness of the repentant brother.

options.text: To rebuke him firmly for his sin.
options.note: Rebuke is part of it, but the emphasis falls on forgiving him when he repents.

options.text: To forgive him only if he proves he has changed.
options.note: Jesus ties forgiveness to repentance expressed, not to proof of lasting change.

options.text: To cut him off after repeated offenses.
options.note: The opposite: forgive even seven times in a day.

quiz.q: What does Jesus teach when the apostles ask Him to increase their faith?

options.text: That faith as small as a mustard seed is enough to do the impossible.
options.note: Luke 17:6 shifts the focus from the amount of faith to its reality and object.

options.text: That great faith can uproot trees and move obstacles.
options.note: True of the image, but the point is that even tiny faith suffices, not that faith must be great.

options.text: That they should work to build up a large store of faith.
options.note: Jesus redirects them away from measuring quantity toward small, genuine trust.

options.text: That they do not have enough faith to be His disciples.
options.note: He encourages them that even the smallest true faith is mighty.

quiz.q: What sets the one returning leper apart from the other nine?

options.text: He came back praising God and fell at Jesus' feet in thanks, and to him alone Jesus said his faith had made him well.
options.note: Luke 17:15-19 marks his grateful return and the word of salvation to him.

options.text: He was the only one who was truly healed.
options.note: All ten were cleansed; the difference is that only he returned in gratitude.

options.text: He returned to give thanks, unlike the nine.
options.note: True, but it omits that Jesus pronounced him well, or saved, in a fuller sense.

options.text: He obeyed the command to show himself to the priest.
options.note: All were told to go to the priests; his distinction was coming back to worship.

quiz.q: What does Jesus say about when the kingdom of God comes?

options.text: It does not come with observable signs, for it is already in their midst in Him.
options.note: Luke 17:20-21 locates the kingdom in Jesus' present, not in a spectacle to spot.

options.text: It will not arrive with visible signs to look for.
options.note: True, but it leaves out the positive claim that the kingdom is already present among them.

options.text: It will come at a time no one can ever know.
options.note: The stress here is on its present arrival in Christ, not merely on an unknown timing.

options.text: It will come only when people spot the right signs.
options.note: Jesus says precisely the opposite; it does not come with signs to be observed.

quiz.q: What will the day of the Son of Man be like?

options.text: Sudden and unmistakable like lightning, coming on an unready world as in the days of Noah and Lot.
options.note: Luke 17:24-30 pictures a sudden, universal, unexpected day.

options.text: A day of sudden judgment on those caught unaware.
options.note: True, but it omits the lightning-like visibility and universality of the day.

options.text: A hidden event that only insiders will notice.
options.note: The opposite: it will flash across the whole sky, seen by all.

options.text: Something to be found by chasing reports of 'here' and 'there'.
options.note: Jesus warns them not to chase such reports; the day needs no such search.

questions: Jesus commands forgiveness even seven times a day. Is there someone whose repeated failures have worn out your willingness to forgive, and what would tireless forgiveness look like there?
The apostles wanted more faith, but Jesus pointed to faith like a seed. Are you waiting to feel strong enough to trust God, when He asks only for the small, real faith you already have?
Nine walked away healed; one came back to worship. When God answers your prayers, do you return to give thanks, or move on and forget?
Jesus says the kingdom is already in your midst. Where might you be scanning the horizon for God while missing His nearness in Christ right now?
Remember Lot's wife. What part of your old life are you tempted to keep looking back at, and what would it mean to hold this life loosely for the day of the Son of Man?

translationNotes.note: The detail 'and he was a Samaritan' is the sting of the story: the only one who returned to thank Jesus was a foreigner and a religious outsider.

'In your midst' can also be rendered 'within you' or 'within your grasp'. Spoken to hostile Pharisees, it most likely means the kingdom stands among them in the person of Jesus, already present rather than arriving as a spectacle.

The BSB omits verse 36, moving from verse 35 to 37, because the earliest and best manuscripts do not contain it. Some later manuscripts and the Textus Receptus add, 'Two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left,' drawn from Matthew 24:40. Its absence changes nothing of the teaching.
